title: SRE SLOs, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning and forecasting, reliability initiatives and incident review standards, required operational tooling, and canonical runbooks used by on-call SREs. It consolidates best practices and templates for teams owning customer-facing inference services (examples: redwood-api, routing-service, proxy-gateway, inference-runtime).

Scope: applies to all production services that serve customer inference traffic (hosted API, dedicated, private control-plane). Does not replace team-specific runbooks - it provides a standard template and required controls.

Goals
- Provide consistent SLO definitions and error budget policies across services so product and SRE can make aligned tradeoffs.
- Ensure predictable capacity planning and automated scaling thresholds to meet throughput and latency SLOs.
- Standardize incident reviews and reliability initiatives so improvements are tracked, prioritized, and measured.
- Maintain a minimal, well-tested runbook set that allows first responders to mitigate and restore service quickly.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- Customer-centric SLIs: choose metrics that map to customer experience (API availability, end-to-end latency, token-generation correctness where applicable).
- Simplicity: small number of SLOs per service (2–4 max), with clear ownership.
- Measurability: every SLO must have a defined instrumentation path and dashboard.

Required SLOs (standard definitions)
- Availability (user-facing): 99.95% monthly uptime for redwood-api and proxy-gateway (exclusion window: scheduled maintenance with 72h advance notice). SLI = successful HTTP 2xx/3xx responses for authenticated requests, weighted by request type.
- Latency (tail): p99 <= 500ms for control-plane operations (e.g., model selection, routing). For inference-runtime, use p95 <= 250ms for cached short prompts and p99 <= 2s for end-to-end generation on hosted small models (document model-specific SLO overrides in model-onboarding pages).
- Error rate: <0.1% client-visible server errors (5xx) aggregated monthly.
- Data integrity / correctness: for evaluation-critical routes, maintain regression test pass-rate >= 99% on the daily eval suite.

Error budget policy
- Error budget = (1 - SLO) * measurement window (monthly). For Availability 99.95% => monthly budget = 0.05% * minutes_in_month.
- Burn rate monitoring: an automated burn-rate alert must be configured:
  - Medium alert: burn rate > 2x for 1 hour (pager to oncall optional, slack channel notification required).
  - High alert (pager): burn rate > 8x for 15 minutes - paging policy runs and mitigation playbook begins.
- Actions on burn:
  1. If burn rate triggers high alert, pause non-essential releases for affected services and add mitigation owners.
  2. If monthly remaining error budget < 25%, product and SRE must jointly approve any risky rollout/change to that service.
  3. If error budget exhausted, initiate error-budget escalation: freeze customer-impacting experiments, increase capacity/route to safer model variant, run traffic shaping.

2) Capacity Planning and Forecasting

Ownership and cadence
- SRE owns cluster-level capacity forecasts; product/engineering owners own per-service traffic forecasts.
- Quarterly capacity review: include traffic growth projections, new feature load, model changes (larger context windows), and expected model onboarding.
- Monthly operational capacity check: review current utilization, critical headroom, and scaling events in last 30 days.

Key metrics to track
- GPU utilization by pool (avg, p95), GPU memory fragmentation, pod/container CPU and memory, request queue depth, scheduling latency, KV-cache hit rate, batching efficiency (tokens/sec/GPU).
- Traffic metrics: rps, tokens/sec, average and p99 sequence length, request size distribution.
- Headroom: maintain soft headroom target of 25% free capacity per pool during business hours for hosted API (configurable by region).

Forecasting methodology
1. Baseline demand = last-90-day moving average + seasonal adjustment.
2. Add uplift for planned launches (provided by product) and model-specific multipliers (large-context = x1.4 token cost).
3. Convert token-rate forecast into GPU-hours using model profiling table (link to quantization-profiles).
4. Run cost/latency tradeoff analysis for choices: dedicated vs. hosted, quantization profile, batching window.

Scaling & autoscaling rules (defaults)
- CPU-based autoscaler for control-plane components (target utilization 65% with cooldown 180s).
- Custom inference autoscaler for runtime pools using tokens/sec per GPU and queue latency: scale up when queue latency > 200ms for more than 120s; scale down only if queue latency < 50ms and utilization < 40% for 10 minutes.
- Reserve buffer for rolling upgrades: do not drive utilization above 70% when performing cluster upgrades; schedule maintenance windows if expected utilization > 60%.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Definition: reliability initiatives are discrete projects that reduce incident frequency, reduce MTTR, or lower cost while preserving SLOs. Examples: prefix caching improvements, KV cache resiliency, automated cold-start mitigation for inference-runtime, and rollout of quantized model variants with verified quality.

Initiative lifecycle
- Proposal: Engineering team submits an Initiative RFC including target metric (e.g., reduce p99 latency by 20% or reduce deploy-induced incidents by 50%).
- Triage: SRE reviews for runbook coverage, monitoring, and rollback strategy.
- Implementation: assign owner, define milestones, include load-testing gating.
- Measurement: define alpha/beta rollout, monitor SLO / error budget impact for 30 days post-rollout.
- Close: produce short results summary and link to postmortem if incident-driven.

Prioritization criteria
- Impact to customer-visible SLOs or significant cost savings (>10% infra cost reduction).
- Risk and rollback complexity.
- Effort (low/medium/high) and cross-team dependencies.

4) Incident Review Standards

Principles
- Blameless culture: focus on system fixes and process improvement.
- Timely reviews: every Sev 2+ incident requires a documented incident review within 7 business days; Sev 1 within 3 business days.
- Actionable outcomes: each incident review must include at least one owner-assigned action with acceptance criteria or a mitigation plan.

Incident review template (minimum fields)
- Title, severity, start and end time, services impacted, summary of customer impact.
- Timeline: ordered events with timestamps. Who did what and when (human and automated actions).
- Root cause analysis (RCA): what failed and why - trace to contributing factors (code, infra, process, third-party).
- Detection and response metrics: time to detection, time to mitigate, time to restore.
- Actions: list of follow-ups, owners, deadlines, and verification steps.
- Postmortem review: announced to stakeholders and included in reliability initiatives backlog if required.

RCA standards
- Use 5 whys to trace immediate cause to underlying systemic issues.
- For incidents with high customer impact, include downstream verification that fix prevented recurrence (e.g., load test or canary).

5) Operational Tooling Requirements

Dashboards and alerts
- Every SLO must have a dashboard showing SLI, rolling error budget consumption, and burn-rate visualization.
- Standard dashboard templates: Service Overview, Latency Breakdown (p50/p95/p99), Error Distribution, Capacity Utilization, and Recent Deploys.
- Alert categorization: Info (Slack), Warning (Slack + email), Critical (PagerDuty page). Provide examples in the templates folder.

Logging & Tracing
- Correlate traces across proxy-gateway -> routing-service -> inference-runtime using request-id header. Save sample traces for incidents for 30 days.
- Structured logs: JSON with fields {request_id, service, route, model, latency_ms, status_code}. Retain critical logs for 90 days.

Chaos & load testing
- Every major change to routing or autoscaler must be gate-tested with a synthetic traffic run in staging that simulates realistic sequence length distribution and token rates.
- Periodic chaos experiments (quarterly) to validate graceful degradation strategies and fallback paths.

Tooling checklist for teams
- SLI exporter configured and validated.
- SLO dashboards and burn rate alerts created from templates.
- Runbooks in Confluence with clear steps and commands.
- Postmortem template available for incident review.

6) Canonical SRE Runbook (template + example)

Runbook naming: service-runbook-<service-name>-<primary-symptom>

Template sections
- Symptom / trigger: what the on-call sees (e.g., sustained p99 latency > 2s, >2% 5xx rate).
- Impact: what customers see and which routes/models are affected.
- Owner & escalation: primary oncall, L2 owner, engineering owner, product contact.
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered): short commands and safe fallbacks.
- Investigate (ordered): logs/traces to inspect, dashboards to open, hypothesis checklist.
- Post-incident steps: preserve artifacts, start incident review, schedule follow-ups.

Example: high 5xx on routing-service
- Symptom: routing-service 5xx rate > 1% for >10 minutes; burn rate high.
- Quick mitigations:
  1. Verify deploys: check CI/CD recent deploys in the last 30 minutes. Command: `kubectl get deploy -n routing-service --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp`
  2. Rollback last deploy if it matches timeframe: `kubectl rollout undo deploy/routing-service --namespace routing-service` (coordinate with product if rollout includes feature flags).
  3. If error is downstream (inference-runtime), switch traffic to fallback model variant: use rollout control-plane UI or CLI `redwoodctl traffic route --service inference-runtime --variant quantized-safe --percent 100` (replace with internal CLI).
  4. If load-related, scale up inference pool: `scale-inference-pool --pool gpu-pool-eu-west --count +2` and notify capacity-oncall.
- Investigation checklist:
  - Check trace for largest latencies: open trace explorer with request-id examples.
  - Inspect pod logs for OOM or repeated exceptions.
  - Check queue depth and batching efficiency metrics.

Runbook testing and ownership
- Runbooks must be exercised during game days at least twice per year.
- Each runbook has a documented owner (team + individual) and last-tested date in the runbook header.

7) Metrics and Reporting

Monthly SRE report must include: SLO attainment per service, error budget consumption and actions taken, top 5 incidents with impact summary, capacity utilization heatmap, and a list of active reliability initiatives with status. Distribute to engineering leadership and product stakeholders.

8) Governance and Exceptions

Exceptions: teams may request an SLO deviation or different error-budget policy for model-specific constraints (e.g., very high variability of latency for long-context models). Exceptions require written approval from SRE manager and product manager and must include compensating controls (additional monitoring, stricter canary policies).

Audit: annual audit of SLO coverage and runbook completeness; teams missing required runbooks will be put on a remediation plan with SRE support.
